To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the composition of root endophytic and rhizo-sphere bacterial communities associated with canola roots differed among three canola cultivar (B. rapa, B. napu, B. nap. x B. rapa), and that these differences may be due to the genetic engineering of the B. napus cultivar.

the root‐endophytic bacterial communities of three canola cultivar differed in composition, and that the bacterial community of the genetically engineered cultivar, Quest differed in composition compared to its parent cultivar, Excel.
the composition of root-endophyte communities of transgenic B. napu s cv. Quest differs from that of non-transgenic cultivars.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of plant breeding on the composition and diversity of bacterial communities associated with the roots.
the effects of plant breeding programs on the composition and diversity of root-endophytes, and their potential to influence crop productivity.
the development of a molecular diagnostic method for the detection of transgenic canola plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the root-endophyte community is influenced by plant factors such as exudation, but the effect of plant breeding programs is less clear.
the composition of bacterial community associated with the roots and rhizosphere of the transgenic canola cultivar Quest was different from the two non‐transgenic cultivars, Parkland and Excel.
the composition of root-endophytism of canola is influenced by cultivar and that this influence is cultivar dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the root endophytic bacterial community associated with the transgenic cultivars, Quest, differed from the non-transgenic canola cultivars, Excel and Parkland, in terms of the diversity and abundance of certain bacterial groups.
transgenic plants may have a different bacterial root community composition than non-transgenic plants, but this is likely not due to the presence of the transgenes themselves.
the root interior and rhizosphere of the transgenic canola cultivar, Quest (B. napus), was different from the non‐transgenics B. napus and B. rapas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the composition of root-endophyte bacterial communities is cultivar dependent, and that the root-endophyte community of a transgenic cultivar is distinct from that of its non-transgenic counterpart.
the root-endophyte community of transgenic canola is distinct from that of non-transgenic canola.
the composition of root-endophyte communities can be altered by genetic engineering, but that these changes are not necessarily negative.
